paras: The shooting of W. M. Goss was a nonfatal shooting near Tyler, Texas, in August 1880, in which Goss, described as "a well-to-do freedman," was shot in the breast by his son-in-law, John Jeffers. Jeffers, reported to have been drunk, was arrested by Sheriff Butler and jailed, and the shooting was noted in a single line of a state-news column.

According to the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman of 19 August 1880, Goss lived near Tyler and was shot "Tuesday," most likely 17 August, though the column gathered items from other papers and did not give a date. The bullet struck him in the breast, and the paper described him as "seriously injured." The shooter was his son-in-law, John Jeffers, "who was intoxicated"; the report gives neither Jeffers's race nor any motive.
Sheriff Butler "captured the assassin and lodged him in jail." No later report on Goss's recovery, an indictment or a trial of Jeffers was found.

The shooting reached print as one unheadlined sentence in the Statesman's "Texas Facts and Fancies" column, set among notes on cotton worms, rains, railroads, robberies and a jail escape. The item identified Goss by his status as a prosperous "freedman" and called Jeffers "the assassin," but offered no comment. No other white paper and no Black paper in the coverage carried the story.
